proved_step: For any finite graph G=(V,L⊔R), let M have rows indexed by X⊆L and columns by Y⊆R, with M[X,Y]=1 iff X∪Y is a perfect matching. Let B be the vertices incident to at least one edge of L and at least one edge of R. Over every field, rank(M)≤2^{|B|}. Proof: A row indexed by X is zero unless X is a matching and covers every vertex incident only to L; likewise a column Y is zero unless Y is a matching and covers every vertex incident only to R. For nonzero rows and columns, X∪Y is a perfect matching exactly when the subsets of B covered by X and Y are disjoint and have union B. Thus compatibility depends only on the subset of B covered by X. Any two nonzero rows whose X cover the same subset of B agree on every column; zero rows also contribute no rank. There are at most 2^{|B|} distinct nonzero rows, so the row rank, hence the rank, is at most 2^{|B|}. This does not establish a lower bound for perfect matching or close a Route F obligation.

statement_start: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), the satisfying assignments of Phi_G = AND_{uv in E} EXACT1(x_u,x_v,z_uv) project onto exactly the independent sets of G, and each projected assignment has a unique extension to the z variables.
statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), the satisfying assignments of Phi_G = AND_{uv in E} EXACT1(x_u,x_v,z_uv) project onto exactly the independent sets of G, and each projected assignment has a unique extension to the z variables. Proof: Fix an assignment x to V. For an edge uv, the equation x_u+x_v+z_uv=1 with all variables Boolean has a solution z_uv iff x_u+x_v<=1, equivalently not both endpoints are selected. When it has a solution, it is uniquely z_uv=1-x_u-x_v. Thus a satisfying extension exists iff x is an independent set, and then all auxiliary values are uniquely determined edge by edge. This also covers E empty, where every x is independent and there is exactly one empty assignment to z. Hence the projection is precisely the independent-set family and is bijective on extensions. This repairs the encoding boundary only; it does not establish any d-SDNNF lower bound or circuit lower bound.

proved_step: statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), let Psi_G = AND_{v in V} EXACT1(y_e : e incident to v), with one Boolean variable y_e per edge. The satisfying assignments of Psi_G are exactly the incidence vectors of perfect matchings of G. Proof: An assignment satisfying Psi_G selects exactly one incident edge at each vertex. Hence every vertex is covered, and no two selected edges share a vertex, so the selected edges form a perfect matching. Conversely, the incidence vector of any perfect matching selects exactly one incident edge at each vertex and satisfies every constraint. If G has an isolated vertex, both sets are empty. If G is empty, both consist of the unique empty assignment/matching. For cubic G, Psi_G has |E| variables, |V| constraints, and each variable occurs in exactly two constraints.

proved_step: statement: Lemma (cubic matching CNF encoding). Let G=(V,E) be a finite simple 3-regular graph, with one Boolean variable y_e for each edge. For each vertex v with incident edges e_1,e_2,e_3, encode EXACT1(y_e1,y_e2,y_e3) by the four clauses (y_e1 OR y_e2 OR y_e3), (NOT y_e1 OR NOT y_e2), (NOT y_e1 OR NOT y_e3), and (NOT y_e2 OR NOT y_e3). The resulting CNF has |E| variables, 4|V| clauses, clause width 2 or 3, and exactly six literal occurrences of each variable. Its satisfying assignments are exactly the incidence vectors of perfect matchings of G. Proof: The positive clause requires at least one incident edge variable to be true, and the three negative pair clauses prohibit two from being true. Together they require exactly one selected edge at v. Applying this at every vertex says precisely that the selected edges cover each vertex once, which is the definition of a perfect matching. Conversely, a perfect matching selects exactly one incident edge at every vertex, so satisfies all four clauses there. Each edge variable occurs in the four-clause block at each of its two endpoints; in each block it appears once positively and twice negatively, hence six literal occurrences total. Each block contributes four clauses, giving 4|V| clauses. This establishes the CNF encoding and its size/occurrence parameters only; it does not establish a d-SDNNF lower bound or any circuit lower bound.

proved_step: statement_start: For every finite simple graph G that is a disjoint union of even cycles and has n vertices, the Boolean perfect-matching function on edge variables has a deterministic decomposable NNF of size O(n). Proof: Write the components as cycles C_i of lengths 2k_i. Each C_i has exactly two perfect matchings, the two alternating edge sets A_i and B_i. For each matching M among these, form the term T_M that contains y_e for e in M and ¬y_e for every other edge of C_i. Set F_i=T_A_i∨T_B_i. Each term fixes all edge variables of C_i, so it accepts exactly one assignment; the two terms are disjoint, hence the disjunction is deterministic. Each term is a conjunction of distinct edge literals, so decomposable. A cycle has 2k_i literals per term, hence F_i has O(k_i) NNF nodes. Set F=∧_i F_i. Distinct components have disjoint edge-variable sets, so this conjunction is decomposable. An assignment satisfies F iff on each component it is one of that cycle's two alternating matchings, which is equivalent to being a perfect matching of G. Summing the O(k_i) sizes gives O(Σ_i k_i)=O(n).
